newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Canadian bonds trail Australia, NZ in dollar bloc.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Canadian bonds trail Australia, NZ in dollar bloc.

text.p: Canadian bonds are being weighed down by expecations of a near-term rise in official interest rates and have little to offer the international investor, while Australia, the U.S. and New Zealand have greater appeal, economists said on Wednesday.

"There is nowhere to go on the Canada/U.S. spread, but with Australia I do not think a test of parity on a three-month horizon could be ruled out," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.
Ten-year Canadian bonds were yielding 23 basis points below T-notes at 1100 GMT, and Australian bonds were quoted at 44 basis points over.
The 30-year benchmark Canadian bond reached an all-time record low yield of 6.395 percent on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Australia cut official interest rates for the fifth time this year on Wednesday, to five percent, surprising markets with the timing of the cut.
Further interest rate cuts are likely in Australia, while a further interest rate rise in Canada is also probable, analysts said.
"Canada may move on interest rates in the next month or so, where the U.S. looks unlikely to move in August," said James Mitchell, senior strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"In Australia we can have another 50 basis points off rates," he added.

The Bank of Canada would be prepared to act independently of the U.S. in raising rates, as it did before, analysts said. Canada raised the call rate range to 3.0-3.5 percent from 2.75-3.25 percent on June 26.

"There is weakness in the Canadian dollar and the underlying economy is picking up some strength, which is testing the Bank of Canada's resistance to raising rates," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking.
The current strong performance of Canadian bonds reflects a global, rather than a domestic trend, analysts said.
"There is yield compression everywhere -- everybody is going for these yields and eating them up," said Gibbs.
Economists put Canada at the bottom of the dollar bloc performance table, but are divided on the front-runner.
Lewis favoured Australia, though he said the case for further easing was not clear-cut.
"There is a probability that this will be the last rate cut in the cycle, but there is an outside chance that if the economy remains weak we will get another cut.

"But the currency seems to have stabilised towards the top of the range, there is not much inflation in sight and growth seems to be quite steady -- that adds up to quite a good case for the bond market."
Gibbs saw the U.S. vying with Australia for lead position.

"The Australian bond market should do pretty well, but it's hard to argue against Treasuries -- the refunding announcment tonight might show a smaller auction size for 10-years, we have the budget deal, and a possible U.S. rate rise is already in the price."
The U.S.'s third quarter refunding auction schedule will be announced at 1700 GMT.
Mitchell put New Zealand in pole position.
"New Zealand has the best fundamental story. If the currency stabilises around these levels, interest rates could come down."
But Lewis was wary of New Zealand markets.
"New Zealand is a terribly volatile story. I would not want to bet on New Zealand politics -- the political background has been more unsettled since they went to proportional representation."
